summary: For ages 11–13: teach the dinosaur-to-bird transition as evidence-weighing of a genuine scientific debate. Learners assemble a case from named feathered theropods (Sinosauropteryx, Anchiornis, Microraptor, Archaeopteryx), discover that feathers predate flight, and compare the cursorial 'ground-up' and arboreal 'trees-down' hypotheses for the origin of flight, weighing fossil and biomechanical evidence rather than deferring to authority.
misconceptions: 'Feathers evolved for flight' — they appeared earlier, likely for insulation/display, and were later co-opted for flight.
'Archaeopteryx is the single direct ancestor of all birds' — it is one transitional form illustrating the pattern.
'The origin of flight is settled' — ground-up and trees-down hypotheses are still debated.
'All feathered dinosaurs could fly' — many had feathers but were flightless.
'Birds evolved from pterosaurs / flying reptiles' — pterosaurs are a separate group; birds arose within theropods.

activities.title: Build the evidence board: specimens on a timeline and a family tree
steps: Place four real fossils on a timeline using approximate ages, and also on a simplified theropod family tree: Anchiornis (about 160 million years ago; well-preserved feathers, with colour reconstructed from preserved melanosomes), Archaeopteryx (about 150 million years ago; the mosaic), Sinosauropteryx (about 125 million years ago; the first non-avian dinosaur found with simple filament 'protofeathers'), and Microraptor (about 120 million years ago; four-winged, often interpreted as a glider, though whether it could also flap and fly is debated).
For each specimen, state the distinct clue it contributes to the dinosaur-to-bird story.

Using where the feathered, flightless theropods branch on the family tree relative to flying forms, write one sentence explaining why feathers appeared before powered flight. Note that a fossil's age shows when that animal lived, not when its feature first evolved: Sinosauropteryx is younger than Archaeopteryx, yet it belongs to an earlier-branching group.
Explain what selection pressure (e.g. insulation or display) could have favoured feathers before any flight use.
activities.insight: Feathers evolved before flight — likely for insulation or display — and were later co-opted for lift; the transition is shown by a pattern across several independent fossils, not one specimen.

activities.title: Weigh the two flight-origin hypotheses
steps: State the ground-up (cursorial) hypothesis: running and leaping from the ground, flapping proto-wings for lift.
State the trees-down (arboreal) hypothesis: climbing and gliding down from height (e.g. Microraptor).
Give at least one line of fossil or biomechanical evidence that each hypothesis draws on.
Explain how an unexpected fossil like four-winged Microraptor bears on the debate.
Explain in your own words why the question is decided by weighing evidence rather than by authority or preference — and why scientists currently hold it open.
activities.insight: The origin of avian flight is a live, evidence-weighed debate between cursorial and arboreal hypotheses; good reasoning lays out the evidence each side cites and keeps uncertainty explicit rather than declaring a winner.

activities.title: Interview the researchers (nature-of-science companion)
steps: Interview a researcher who backs the ground-up hypothesis and one who backs trees-down.
Ask each: 'What is your best evidence?' and 'What would change your mind?'
Compare their answers and identify where the evidence genuinely conflicts versus where they agree.
Summarise how holding a question open while weighing fossils differs from simply picking a favourite.
activities.insight: A genuine scientific debate is settled by evidence and remains open until the evidence decides; scientists can disagree while reasoning from the same fossil record.

activities.title: Flight lab: test anatomy against lift (scaffold)
steps: Take a feathered theropod and attempt a launch two ways: sprinting and leaping from the ground flapping proto-wings, and climbing then gliding down from a tree.
Adjust wing area, feather type and launch mode, and observe which anatomy generates sustained lift for a given body.
Watch a balance/support meter weigh the accumulating support for each hypothesis as fossil evidence and lab results are added.
Note which outcomes seem to favour ground-up and which favour trees-down, and connect this back to the fossil evidence board.
Record what the simulation cannot settle on its own — i.e. which real fossils would be needed to decide.
activities.insight: Biomechanics (wing area, feather type, launch mode) interacts with hypothesis testing: different anatomies suit different launch strategies, which is why the debate turns on both fossils and mechanics.

activities.title: Check: match specimens and categorise evidence
steps: Match each specimen to the clue it provides: Sinosauropteryx ↔ simple filaments (the first non-avian dinosaur found with them); Anchiornis ↔ detailed feathers with reconstructed colour; Microraptor ↔ four-winged, probable glider; Archaeopteryx ↔ transitional mosaic.
Sort given lines of evidence as supporting ground-up versus trees-down.
Answer: why does feathers-appearing-before-flight matter for the whole debate?

Tier A: name a feathered theropod and its clue. Tier B: explain why feathers before flight matters. Tier C: state both hypotheses, give one line of evidence for each, and explain how evidence (not authority) decides.
activities.insight: Secure recall of which fossil contributes which clue, and the ability to classify evidence by hypothesis, supports but does not replace constructing the argument.

checkQuestion: Archaeopteryx has feathers and a wishbone like a bird, but also teeth, clawed hands, and a long bony tail like a dinosaur. Why do scientists treat a 'halfway' fossil like this as strong evidence for the dinosaur-to-bird transition — rather than it just being a weird one-off animal?
checkAnswer: Because a mix of dinosaur and bird features is exactly what a transitional form should show, and it doesn't stand alone — many feathered theropods (e.g. Sinosauropteryx, Anchiornis, Microraptor) fill in the sequence, so several independent fossils show the gradual acquisition of bird features. The pattern across many fossils, not one specimen, makes it strong evidence.
